subject: Weighting estimates from strata by effort or area

messages.author: 54c94f7c2bf78491
messages.subject: Weighting estimates from strata by effort or area
parts:
Hello distance-sampling,

In the Distance R package, it is possible to stratify using a unique Region.Label in the Region Table (or flatfile) for each desired strata. When doing so, an estimate for density and abundance is produced for each strata, and when summarizing the output of ds(), a line for total is produced, which for density appears to be the mean of the strata-level estimates, and for abundance, the sum.

> head(full.region.table)
  Region.Label      Area
1         2010 1.807e+09
2       2011_H 9.030e+08
3       2011_L 9.030e+08 

Density:
    Label     Estimate           se        cv          lcl          ucl        df
1    2010 3.915790e-07 1.578621e-07 0.4031424 1.798536e-07 8.525492e-07  53.92967
2  2011_H 1.291807e-06 3.673908e-07 0.2844007 7.347620e-07 2.271164e-06  38.68982
3  2011_L 7.861817e-07 4.622038e-07 0.5879096 2.540084e-07 2.433312e-06  22.04769
...
10  Total 7.788055e-07 1.555369e-07 0.1997122 5.276607e-07 1.149485e-06 277.12378

In Distance for Windows, there is an option to set the global density estimate/pooled density estimates as the mean or sum of strata, and to weight the mean by area or by effort. 

Is the total row in the R package equivilent to a pooled density estimate in Distance for Windows? Is there any documentation on how the totals are weighted by default in the R package? What is the default? Is there a way to specify weighting in the R package?

(Note in the above example output using a total wouldn't make sense as there are multiple years, but this would be used where combining strata estimates to produce a total is valid...)

Cheers,

Olly

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Weighting estimates from strata by effort or area
parts:
Olly

The short answer to your questions is that weighting of strata is not possible with the current version of ds() in the Distance package.  The default is for the "Total" to be equivalent to a pooled estimate in Distance for Windows.

You can prove this to yourself by using the "minke" dataset included in the Distance R package.  The identical data exist in the "Stratify Example.dst" sample project that ships with Distance for Windows.  The only challenge in proving this to yourself is that group sizes are associated with the Distance for Windows project, but the "minke" dataset treats each detection as a singleton.  Nevertheless, adjusting the Stratify Example.dst project to use exact distances, treat all group sizes as 1 and set up this stratification analysis

(pooled detection function)

 Stratum: 1. Ideal Habitat                                 
 Half-normal/Cosine    
                 D      0.45950E-01   24.47    14.74 0.27461E-01  0.76889E-01
                 N       3906.0       24.47    14.74  2334.0       6536.0   
 Stratum: 2. Marginal Habitat                              
 Half-normal/Cosine    
                 D      0.21228E-01   38.95    11.91 0.93528E-02  0.48183E-01
                 N       12737.       38.95    11.91  5612.0       28910.   

 Pooled Estimates:
                         Estimate      %CV     df     95% Confidence Interval
                        ------------------------------------------------------
                 D      0.24296E-01   30.71    13.38 0.12726E-01  0.46384E-01
                 N       16643.       30.71    13.38  8718.0       31773.   

you will produce the same AIC score, estimate of the sigma of the detection function and stratum-specific and combined density estimates as this R analysis of the "minke" dataset:

library(Distance)
data(minke)
summary(ds(data=minke))

Check me to see that is correct.

Thanks again,

 

Olly
